questions.stem: What are standing orders?
questions.why: Standing orders are written protocols that serve as offline medical control — pre-approved actions a provider can take without calling in first.

options.t: A hospital's internal staffing schedule
options.why: Staffing schedules have nothing to do with medical direction or protocols.

options.t: Verbal orders given only over the radio in real time
options.why: Real-time verbal radio orders describe online, not offline, medical control.

options.t: A list of medications a patient takes at home
options.why: A home medication list is part of patient history, not a form of medical direction.

options.t: Protocols that function as offline medical control

questions.stem: Is online medical control only used for approving medication administration?
questions.why: Online direct medical control isn't just for med approval — it's also a resource to consult on treatments a provider wants a second opinion on.

options.t: No, it exists purely for after-the-fact legal documentation
options.why: This isn't primarily a legal-documentation tool — it's a clinical consultation resource.

options.t: Yes, approving medication administration is its one and only job
options.why: Limiting it strictly to medication approval undersells its broader consult role.

options.t: No — it's also used to consult on treatments you're unsure about
No, its only real function is relaying dispatch information along
options.why: Relaying dispatch information isn't the function of online medical control.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of the '6 rights' of medication administration?
questions.why: The 6 rights are patient, dose, drug, time, route, and documentation — route is one of the six.

options.t: Right family consent
options.why: Family consent isn't one of the six specific rights in this framework.

options.t: Right route
Right insurance
options.why: Insurance status isn't one of the six rights checked before giving a medication.

options.t: Right ambulance unit
options.why: Which ambulance unit responded isn't part of this medication-safety checklist.

questions.stem: What is the difference between antiseptics and disinfectants?
questions.why: Antiseptics are used for invasive procedures on the patient, while disinfectants are toxic to living tissue and are used on equipment and surfaces instead.

options.t: Antiseptics go on the patient; disinfectants are toxic to tissue
Disinfectants are safe to apply directly on skin, unlike antiseptics
options.why: This reverses the actual relationship — disinfectants are the ones considered toxic to living tissue.

options.t: Antiseptics kill bacteria while disinfectants kill viruses
options.why: Both act across a broad range of organisms — the split is where each can safely be used, not which organism it kills.

options.t: Antiseptics sterilize equipment; disinfectants prep the skin
options.why: That is backwards: antiseptics are the skin-safe ones, and disinfectants are reserved for surfaces and equipment.

questions.stem: What is sterile technique?
questions.why: Sterile technique means the deconstruction of all living organisms using heat, gas, or chemicals — a more rigorous standard than simple cleaning.

options.t: Wearing gloves alone, with no other precaution taken
options.why: Gloves alone don't constitute the full sterile technique being defined here.

options.t: Deconstruction of all living organisms using heat, gas, or chemicals
Wiping a surface down once with a single alcohol pad
options.why: A single alcohol wipe is a disinfecting action, not the complete sterilization process described.

options.t: Simply washing your hands with ordinary soap and water
options.why: Handwashing alone is a baseline hygiene step, not the full definition of sterile technique.

questions.stem: What is the standard approach to handling any body fluid encountered in the field?
questions.why: The standard is to treat all body fluid as infectious, regardless of appearance or the patient's reported history — a universal precaution.

options.t: Only treat visibly bloody fluid as infectious
options.why: Limiting concern to visibly bloody fluid ignores other body fluids that can also transmit infection.

options.t: Treat all body fluid as infectious
Treat body fluid as infectious only in pediatric patients
options.why: This precaution applies across all patients, not just a pediatric subset.

options.t: Assume fluid is safe unless the patient reports a known infection
options.why: Assuming safety by default is the opposite of the standard precaution approach.

questions.stem: What defines dehydration in this context?
questions.why: Dehydration is inadequate total systemic fluid volume, producing signs like tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, and skin tenting.

options.t: A condition limited strictly to pediatric patients
options.why: Dehydration is not limited to any single age group.

options.t: Excess systemic fluid volume
options.why: Excess volume describes overhydration, the opposite condition.

options.t: Inadequate total systemic fluid volume
A normal fluid volume with abnormal electrolytes only
options.why: Dehydration is specifically a volume problem, not just an isolated electrolyte issue with normal volume.

questions.stem: Which of these is a listed cause of dehydration?
questions.why: Diarrhea, hemorrhage, vomiting, infection, high caffeine intake, and insufficient fluid intake are all listed causes of dehydration.

options.t: Water intoxication
options.why: Water intoxication is specifically listed as an overhydration cause, not a dehydration one.

options.t: Diarrhea
Overhydration from unmonitored IV fluids
options.why: Unmonitored IV fluids leading to overload is a cause of overhydration, not dehydration.

options.t: Kidney failure
options.why: Kidney failure is listed as a cause of overhydration in this framework.

questions.stem: What defines overhydration?
questions.why: Overhydration means the body's systemic fluid volume increases, producing signs like shortness of breath, pitting edema, and crackles or pulmonary edema.

options.t: A rise in total body water with no change in circulating volume
options.why: The circulating volume rises too — that is exactly what produces the edema and the crackles.

options.t: The body's systemic fluid volume increases beyond normal
The body's systemic fluid volume drops below normal
options.why: A drop below normal volume describes dehydration, the opposite condition.

options.t: A normal fluid volume shifted into the wrong compartment
options.why: That describes third spacing. Overhydration is a genuine increase in systemic volume.

questions.stem: Which of these is a listed cause of overhydration?
questions.why: Unmonitored IV fluids (especially in pediatric patients), kidney failure, water intoxication, and prolonged hypoventilation are listed causes of overhydration.

options.t: Hemorrhage, another cause tied to dehydration instead
options.why: Hemorrhage is a dehydration cause, driving fluid volume down rather than up.

options.t: Diarrhea, a cause tied to dehydration instead
options.why: Diarrhea is listed as a cause of dehydration, the opposite fluid problem.

options.t: A high caffeine diet, also a dehydration cause
options.why: A high caffeine diet is listed under dehydration causes, not overhydration.

options.t: Unmonitored IV fluids, especially in pediatric patients

questions.stem: Which of these can alter a patient's electrolyte balance?
questions.why: Vomiting, diarrhea, dietary issues, medications, and blood loss or injuries are all listed as ways electrolytes can become altered.

options.t: Lots of vomiting
Mild seasonal allergies
options.why: Mild seasonal allergies aren't a listed electrolyte-altering factor.

options.t: A routine, uncomplicated night's sleep
options.why: Ordinary sleep isn't a cause of electrolyte imbalance in this framework.

options.t: A single normal meal
options.why: A single normal meal isn't listed as a source of electrolyte disturbance.

questions.stem: What is a crystalloid solution?
questions.why: A crystalloid is dissolved crystals in water — small enough to cross membranes and shift fluid levels throughout the body, unlike a colloid.

options.t: A solution containing no electrolytes, given to dilute the blood
options.why: Crystalloids are defined by their dissolved electrolytes — that is what lets them shift fluid between compartments.

options.t: Dissolved crystals in water that can cross membranes and shift fluid
Molecules too large to pass through capillary membranes
options.why: Large molecules that stay confined to the vasculature describes a colloid, the opposite behavior.

options.t: A solution that holds in the vascular space for several hours
options.why: Crystalloid leaves the vasculature quickly; roughly two-thirds of it has moved into the tissues within an hour.

questions.stem: Why are crystalloid boluses generally given?
questions.why: Crystalloid boluses are given to maintain perfusion, not specifically to raise blood pressure — and too much fluid can actually harm perfusion.

options.t: To help maintain perfusion, not specifically to raise blood pressure
To directly correct an abnormal electrolyte panel
options.why: Correcting the electrolyte panel isn't the primary described purpose of a bolus here.

options.t: To fully replace the need for a blood transfusion in every case
options.why: Crystalloids don't substitute for blood products in every transfusion scenario.

options.t: Specifically and only to raise the patient's blood pressure
options.why: Raising blood pressure directly isn't the stated purpose — maintaining perfusion is.

questions.stem: What defines a colloid solution?
questions.why: A colloid contains large molecules that stay in the vascular space rather than crossing into tissue, and it can cause dramatic fluid shifts with a relatively short duration of action.

options.t: Dissolved crystals in water, identical to a crystalloid
options.why: Dissolved crystals describe a crystalloid, not what makes a colloid distinct.

options.t: Molecules too large to pass through capillary membranes
A solution of electrolytes that crosses membranes freely
options.why: Free movement across the membrane is crystalloid behavior — a colloid's molecules are too large to follow.

options.t: A solution that shifts fluid slowly, over several hours
options.why: Colloids pull fluid into the vasculature dramatically and fast. Their limitation is a short duration of action, not a slow onset.

questions.stem: What characterizes an isotonic solution?
questions.why: An isotonic solution has sodium equal to the cells, so it doesn't cause dramatic fluid movement into or out of them.

options.t: A solution with no sodium at all, so nothing pulls on the cell
options.why: Isotonic means sodium equal to the cell, not absent — free water with no solute is strongly hypotonic and does burst cells.

options.t: Lower sodium than the cells, which pushes fluid into them
options.why: Lower sodium than the cells describes a hypotonic solution.

options.t: Equal sodium to the cells, so no dramatic fluid shift happens
Higher sodium than the cells, which pulls fluid out of them
options.why: Higher sodium than the cells describes a hypertonic solution.

questions.stem: What happens to cells when a hypertonic solution is given?
questions.why: A hypertonic solution has higher sodium than the cell, drawing fluid out of the cell and causing it to shrivel — used to help stabilize BP, increase urine output, and reduce edema.

options.t: The cells rupture as sodium pulls water in behind it
options.why: Sodium outside the cell pulls water out, not in. Hypertonic solutions shrivel cells rather than bursting them.

options.t: Cell volume holds steady while the extracellular volume falls
options.why: Extracellular volume rises, and it rises partly at the cell's expense — the cell shrinks.

options.t: Fluid moves into the cells instead, causing them to swell
options.why: Fluid moving in and causing swelling is the hypotonic effect, the opposite direction.

options.t: Fluid moves out of the cells, causing them to shrivel

questions.stem: What happens to cells when a hypotonic solution is given?
questions.why: A hypotonic solution has lower sodium than the cell, so fluid shifts into the cell, causing it to expand — a sudden shift from the intravascular space into the cells.

options.t: Fluid moves out of the cells, causing them to shrivel
options.why: Fluid moving out and shriveling is the hypertonic effect, the opposite direction.

options.t: Fluid moves into the cells, causing them to expand
Cell volume is unchanged; only the extracellular space expands
options.why: The whole effect of a hypotonic solution is water crossing into the cell, so the cell does swell.

options.t: Water leaves the cell first, then returns as sodium equalizes
options.why: There is no two-phase movement. With less sodium outside than in, water moves into the cell and stays there.

questions.stem: Roughly how much crystalloid fluid is needed to replace a given volume of blood loss?
questions.why: Roughly 3 mL of crystalloid fluid is needed for every 1 mL of blood lost, since crystalloid distributes beyond just the vascular space — and too much can hurt perfusion.

options.t: About 10 mL of fluid for every 1 mL of blood lost
options.why: Ten to one grossly overshoots — that much crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens the bleeding.

options.t: About 3 mL of fluid for every 1 mL of blood lost
An exact 1:1 ratio of fluid to blood lost
options.why: A flat 1:1 ratio doesn't reflect how crystalloid distributes throughout the body compared to blood.

options.t: About 1 mL of fluid for every 3 mL of blood lost
options.why: That is the ratio inverted. Because crystalloid spreads beyond the vessels, you need more fluid than blood lost, not less.

questions.stem: What is infiltration?
questions.why: Infiltration is fluid escaping into the tissue around the IV site rather than staying in the vein, managed by discontinuing the line and applying direct pressure.

options.t: Inflammation developing along the wall of the vein
options.why: Vein inflammation describes thrombophlebitis, a separate complication.

options.t: A mechanical blockage of the vein itself or the catheter
options.why: A blockage describes occlusion, a distinct IV complication.

options.t: A bruise forming right at the site of IV insertion
options.why: A bruise describes a hematoma, a different finding entirely.

options.t: Escape of IV fluid into the tissue surrounding the site

questions.stem: What is occlusion in the context of an IV line?
questions.why: Occlusion is a blockage of the vein or catheter, which can develop from catheter positioning or if blood pressure exceeds the flow rate — managed by trying to clear it or discontinuing the line.

options.t: A bacterial infection introduced through the IV site
options.why: A site infection is a separate complication from a mechanical blockage.

options.t: Fluid escaping into the surrounding tissue
options.why: Fluid escaping into tissue describes infiltration, a distinct complication.

options.t: A blockage of the vein or catheter
Air entering the circulatory system through the line
options.why: Air entering the circulation describes an air embolus, a different problem entirely.

questions.stem: What is thrombophlebitis?
questions.why: Thrombophlebitis is inflammation of the vein, which can be caused by infection and usually shows up as pain, tenderness, and edema hours after starting IV therapy.

options.t: Fluid overload from running the IV bag too fast
options.why: Fluid overload is circulatory overload, a separate complication from thrombophlebitis.

options.t: An immediate bruise appearing right at the puncture site
options.why: An immediate bruise describes a hematoma, a different and more immediate finding.

options.t: A sudden allergic reaction to the IV fluid itself
options.why: An allergic fluid reaction is a distinct complication from vein inflammation.

options.t: Inflammation of the vein, often appearing hours after IV therapy

questions.stem: What are pyrogenic reactions?
questions.why: Pyrogenic reactions come from foreign proteins — often introduced from the IV bag itself — and typically cause fever roughly 30 minutes after the infusion starts.

options.t: A skin reaction that stays confined to the puncture site
options.why: A pyrogenic reaction produces a systemic fever response, not just a localized skin finding.

options.t: A reaction that only happens with a mismatched blood type
options.why: Blood type incompatibility is a distinct, transfusion-specific reaction, not this general pyrogenic one.

options.t: A reaction that only ever occurs with an IM injection route
options.why: Pyrogenic reactions are linked to IV administration, not IM injection specifically.

options.t: Fever from foreign proteins, often traced back to the IV bag

questions.stem: Why is circulatory overload a particular concern for cardiac patients receiving IV fluid?
questions.why: In a cardiac patient, circulatory overload from IV fluid can push the heart and lungs past what they can compensate for, risking pulmonary or renal dysfunction — managed by slowing the rate, raising the head, and giving high-flow oxygen.

options.t: It can push a strained heart and lungs into dysfunction
The failing heart cannot excrete sodium, so fluid is retained
options.why: Sodium handling is a kidney function. The cardiac problem is a ventricle that cannot move the extra volume forward.

options.t: Cardiac medications interact directly with IV crystalloid
options.why: There is no such interaction — the issue is mechanical, a heart that cannot keep up with the added preload.

options.t: The pericardium restricts filling once the volume rises
options.why: Pericardial restriction is a separate problem. Here the ventricle simply cannot move the volume it is handed.

questions.stem: What is the recommended positioning if an air embolus is suspected during IV therapy?
questions.why: For a suspected air embolus, the patient is positioned on their left side with 100% oxygen while being transported — this position helps trap air in the right side of the heart.

options.t: Right side down, so the air rises away from the heart
options.why: Left side down is what traps the air in the right ventricle and keeps it out of the pulmonary outflow tract.

options.t: Left side, with 100% oxygen given, during transport
Prone position, with the legs raised above the heart
options.why: Face-down with the legs up does nothing to keep air out of the pulmonary outflow tract, and it makes ventilation harder.

options.t: Fully upright, sitting with the legs left dangling down
options.why: Sitting upright lets the air rise straight into the pulmonary outflow tract — the opposite of what you want.

questions.stem: What is the difference between enteral and parenteral medication routes?
questions.why: Enteral medications go through the digestive/intestinal tract (oral, suppository) and absorb slowly, while parenteral covers any other route (IV, IM, IO, subcutaneous, transdermal, inhalation) and absorbs faster.

options.t: Enteral covers IV and IO; parenteral covers IM and subcutaneous
options.why: All four of those are parenteral. Enteral means the digestive tract — oral and rectal.

options.t: Parenteral refers only to medications given by mouth
options.why: Parenteral refers to routes other than the digestive tract, not oral medication.

options.t: Enteral goes through the digestive tract; parenteral is any other route
Enteral and parenteral routes absorb at comparable rates
options.why: Enteral absorption runs 30 to 90 minutes against roughly 30 to 60 seconds for IV or IO.

questions.stem: Roughly how quickly are oral medications absorbed compared to IV medications?
questions.why: Oral medications are absorbed slowly (roughly 30–90 minutes), while IV and IO routes act within about 30–60 seconds.

options.t: Oral and IV both absorb on an essentially identical timeline
options.why: These two routes have very different absorption timelines, not identical ones.

options.t: Oral is slower, but only by a minute or two
options.why: The gap is far wider: 30 to 90 minutes for oral against roughly 30 to 60 seconds for IV.

options.t: Oral takes far longer — roughly 30 to 90 minutes versus seconds
Oral doses reach the same peak level, just later
options.why: First-pass metabolism means less of an oral dose reaches circulation at all, so the peak is lower as well as later.

questions.stem: Which mnemonic lists medications that can be given via the endotracheal tube?
questions.why: LEAN — lidocaine, epinephrine, atropine, naloxone — lists medications that can be given through the endotracheal tube when IV/IO access isn't available.

options.t: MONA — morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin
options.why: MONA is a cardiac treatment mnemonic, not related to ET tube medication administration.

options.t: SLUDGEM — a set of cholinergic toxidrome findings
options.why: SLUDGEM describes a toxidrome presentation, not a list of ET-administered drugs.

options.t: LEAN — lidocaine, epinephrine, atropine, naloxone
DOPE — dislodgment, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment
options.why: DOPE is the mnemonic for causes of sudden deterioration in a tubed patient, unrelated to ET drug administration.

questions.stem: Which of these is a listed site for intraosseous (IO) access?
questions.why: The tibia, humeral head, and sternum are the listed IO access sites — bones with accessible marrow for infusion.

options.t: The radial artery
options.why: The radial artery is not an IO site — it's an arterial access/monitoring point.

options.t: The femoral artery
options.why: The femoral artery is an arterial site, not one of the listed IO locations.

options.t: The tibia
The subclavian vein
options.why: The subclavian is a central venous access site, not an IO location.

questions.stem: Which of these is a contraindication to IO access at a given site?
questions.why: A fractured bone, osteoporosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, bilateral knee replacements, and a prosthetic limb are all listed contraindications to IO access at that site.

options.t: Patient anxiety about needles
options.why: Needle anxiety is a psychological factor, not a physical contraindication to IO placement.

options.t: A fracture at that bone
Cold ambient temperature
options.why: Ambient temperature isn't a listed factor affecting IO site selection.

options.t: A recent tattoo near the site
options.why: A nearby tattoo isn't a listed contraindication to IO access.

questions.stem: What is the formula for converting a patient's weight from pounds to kilograms?
questions.why: Divide pounds by 2, then take 10% back off that result. For 200 lb: half is 100, minus 10 is 90 kg — within a pound of the exact 90.7.

options.t: Multiply the number of pounds by 2.2 to get the answer
options.why: Multiplying by 2.2 goes the wrong direction — that converts kilograms back to pounds.

options.t: Simply add 2.2 onto the raw number of pounds given
options.why: Simply adding 2.2 isn't a valid unit conversion at all.

options.t: Just divide the pounds by ten to reach the converted weight
options.why: Dividing by 10 lands nowhere near kilograms — a 200 lb patient would come out as 20 kg.

options.t: Divide the pounds by two, then subtract ten percent of that

questions.stem: What is the desired dose divided by the concentration on hand used to calculate?
questions.why: Volume to administer equals the desired dose (mg) divided by the concentration on hand (mg/mL) — the core volume calculation for any liquid medication.

options.t: The medication's onset of action
options.why: Onset of action is a pharmacokinetic property, not something this calculation produces.

options.t: The patient's weight in kilograms
options.why: Patient weight is a separate input used elsewhere in dosing calculations, not this formula's output.

options.t: The volume to be administered
The total drug concentration in the vial
options.why: Drug concentration is an input to this formula, not what it calculates.

questions.stem: What does 'drug concentration' refer to in medication math?
questions.why: Drug concentration is the total weight (mg) of drug present in a specific volume of solution (mL) — the mg/mL value printed on the vial.

options.t: The total volume of the whole vial, regardless of drug content
options.why: Concentration ties drug weight to a specific volume, not just the vial's total volume alone.

options.t: The specific amount of drug that a physician has ordered
options.why: The amount ordered by the physician is the desired dose, a separate value from concentration.

options.t: The route by which that drug is ultimately going to be given
options.why: Route of administration is unrelated to the concentration value itself.

options.t: The total weight of drug, in mg, inside a given volume in mL

questions.stem: For a continuous drip calculation, which values are multiplied together to find the drops per minute?
questions.why: Three numbers multiply together: the dose the patient needs each minute, the concentration that turns that dose into mL, and the drip set's drops per mL. The result is drops per minute.

options.t: Dose per minute, the concentration in mL, and the set's drop factor
Dose per hour, the total bag volume, and the patient's weight
options.why: Bag volume never enters a rate calculation, and an hourly dose has to be converted to minutes before the drop factor can be applied.

options.t: The set's drop factor and the total bag volume alone
options.why: Without the dose and the concentration there is nothing telling you how much drug each drop carries.

options.t: Dose per minute and the drop factor, without the concentration
options.why: Concentration is what converts a dose in milligrams into a volume in mL — leave it out and the drop factor has nothing to act on.

questions.stem: How is a fluid bolus rate over a specific time period calculated?
questions.why: The formula is fluid amount in the bag divided by the time, multiplied by the drip set's gtts (drops) per mL, giving drops per minute.

options.t: The vial's total volume divided by the patient's age in years
options.why: Patient age isn't a factor in this specific rate calculation.

options.t: Patient weight multiplied together with the desired dose value
options.why: Patient weight and desired dose feed into a different calculation, not this fluid-rate formula.

options.t: Bag fluid amount divided by time, times drops per mL from the set
Concentration on hand multiplied by the chosen administration route
options.why: Route of administration isn't a numeric factor multiplied into this formula.

questions.stem: Which of these is a described tool for determining pediatric medication doses in the field?
questions.why: Length-based resuscitation tapes, pediatric dosing wheels, and EMS field-guide tables all exist for the same reason: a child's dose scales with size, and length estimates weight far better than eyeballing it.

options.t: A generic one-size-fits-all pediatric dose chart with no measurements
options.why: A single flat pediatric dose ignores the tenfold weight range between a newborn and a twelve-year-old.

options.t: The patient's shoe size
options.why: Shoe size isn't a described pediatric dosing tool.

options.t: A standard adult dosing card only
options.why: An adult dosing card doesn't account for the weight-based scaling pediatric dosing requires.

options.t: A length-based resuscitation tape measure

questions.stem: What is bioavailability?
questions.why: Bioavailability is the amount of a given drug that actually makes it into the systemic circulation — a key factor in the absorption step of pharmacokinetics.

options.t: The total dose of drug given regardless of route
options.why: Total dose given is a separate number from how much of it actually reaches circulation.

options.t: The drug's chemical name as opposed to its brand name
options.why: Chemical versus brand naming is a labeling distinction, unrelated to bioavailability.

options.t: The amount of drug that actually makes it into systemic circulation
The concentration listed on the medication vial
options.why: Vial concentration is a fixed label value, not the same as what reaches the bloodstream.

questions.stem: A 44 lb child needs diphenhydramine at 1 mg/kg. The vial is 50 mg/mL. What volume do you draw up?
questions.why: 44 lb ÷ 2 = 22, minus 10% = about 20 kg. At 1 mg/kg that is 20 mg. Volume = 20 mg ÷ 50 mg/mL = 0.4 mL.

options.t: 0.4 mL
0.8 mL
options.why: 0.8 mL would deliver 40 mg, about double what is ordered.

options.t: 0.2 mL
options.why: 0.2 mL would deliver 10 mg, roughly half the required dose.

options.t: 1.0 mL
options.why: 1.0 mL would deliver the full 50 mg, far above the calculated dose.

questions.stem: You must infuse 100 cc over 10 minutes using a 15 gtts/mL drip set. What is the drip rate?
questions.why: Fluid ÷ time × drop factor = (100 cc ÷ 10 min) × 15 gtts/mL = 10 × 15 = 150 drops per minute.

options.t: 150 drops per minute
15 drops per minute
options.why: 15 drops per minute is just the set's drop factor, not a rate.

options.t: 100 drops per minute
options.why: 100 drops per minute ignores the drip set factor entirely.

options.t: 60 drops per minute
options.why: 60 drops per minute does not follow from these particular numbers.

questions.stem: A trauma patient has lost roughly 500 mL of blood. Using the crystalloid replacement ratio, about how much fluid does that correspond to?
questions.why: Crystalloid replaces blood at roughly 3 mL per 1 mL lost, so 500 mL of blood corresponds to about 1,500 mL — while remembering too much fluid can itself harm perfusion.

options.t: 1,500 mL of crystalloid
3,000 mL of crystalloid
options.why: 3,000 mL reflects a 6:1 ratio, double the figure taught.

options.t: 500 mL of crystalloid
options.why: A 1:1 replacement ignores how crystalloid distributes beyond the vasculature.

options.t: 250 mL of crystalloid
options.why: 250 mL is half the volume lost and well under the ratio.

questions.stem: A 220 lb adult is ordered fentanyl at 1 mcg/kg, with a maximum single dose of 100 mcg. What is given?
questions.why: 220 lb ÷ 2 = 110, minus 10% = about 100 kg. At 1 mcg/kg that calculates to 100 mcg, which sits right at the maximum single dose.

options.t: 110 mcg, since that is the calculated dose
options.why: 110 mcg would ignore the stated single-dose ceiling.

options.t: 50 mcg, which is half the maximum allowed
options.why: Halving the maximum is not supported by the order as written.

options.t: 100 mcg, because the calculation exceeds the cap
220 mcg, matching the patient's weight in pounds
options.why: Dosing from pounds skips the required conversion to kilograms.

questions.stem: Which solution would you expect to pull fluid out of the cells and into the vascular space?
questions.why: A hypertonic solution carries more sodium than the cell, so water follows the gradient out of the cell — which is why it can help stabilize BP and reduce edema.

options.t: A colloid-free crystalloid
options.why: That description does not define a tonicity relationship at all.

options.t: An isotonic solution
options.why: An isotonic solution produces no dramatic shift in either direction.

options.t: A hypotonic solution
options.why: A hypotonic solution drives fluid into cells, causing them to swell.

options.t: A hypertonic solution

questions.stem: Several hours after an IV was started, the site is painful, tender, and swollen along the vein. What is this most consistent with?
questions.why: Pain, tenderness and swelling tracking along the vein hours after the IV went in is thrombophlebitis — inflammation of the vessel wall itself, distinct from infiltration's prompt local swelling.

options.t: An air embolus entering the circulation
options.why: An air embolus presents with sudden systemic symptoms, not local tenderness.

options.t: Thrombophlebitis developing at the site
Infiltration of fluid into the tissue
options.why: Infiltration shows up promptly as swelling, not hours later along the vein.

options.t: A pyrogenic reaction from the IV bag
options.why: A pyrogenic reaction causes fever about 30 minutes into the infusion.
